title: Medication and route words
blurb: Read the HESI A2 words for why a drug is given, how it gets into the body and what it does, and beat the prescribe/proscribe and adverse/averse traps.
question: A medication record lists a sublingual tablet, a transdermal patch and a parenteral antibiotic, and warns of one contraindication. Where does each drug enter the body, and what does the warning mean?

teach.body: Formally, medication vocabulary names why a drug is given (indication), why it must not be (contraindication), the route by which it enters the body (oral, sublingual, intravenous) and the effects it produces (efficacy, tolerance, adverse reactions). In plain English: why, why not, where in, and what happens. Most route words are built from a position prefix plus a body-part root, so sub + lingual is simply 'under the tongue'.

rows.label: Meaning
values: a reason not to use it

rows.label: Meaning
values: by a route other than the gut

teach.caption: Parenteral has nothing to do with parents: para- (beside) + enter (intestine).

teach.h: Drug effect and drug class words
head: Word
Meaning
Near miss
rows: ability to produce the intended effect
reduced response, so more drug is needed
needing the drug to function normally
causes loss of sensation or consciousness
an inactive substance given as if a medicine

teach.caption: Also: dilute (weaken with liquid) vs dilate (widen); concentrated is the opposite of dilute.

teach.h: Scenario: Marcus reads a medication record
teach.body: Marcus Lee, an EMT applying to a paramedic program, reads: 'Nitroglycerin sublingual as needed. Fentanyl transdermal patch. Ceftriaxone intramuscular. Allergy to penicillin: contraindication for amoxicillin.' He works it out: one tablet dissolves under the tongue; a patch delivers drug through the skin; one antibiotic is injected into a muscle; and the allergy is a reason not to give amoxicillin. None of these is an indication, which would be a reason to give a drug.

teach.text: The HESI A2 loves near-identical words: prescribe (order) vs proscribe (forbid), adverse (harmful) vs averse (unwilling), efficacy (works) vs efficiency (no waste), potent (strong) vs patent (open), oral (mouth) vs aural (ear), analgesic (pain relief) vs anesthetic (no sensation). Read every letter before you choose.

teach.body: Administer means to give a medication. Dosage is the amount and timing to be taken. Dilute means to make weaker by adding liquid; concentrated means containing a lot of a substance in a small volume. Example: 'The nurse will administer the concentrated drug only after it is diluted in saline.' Do not confuse dilute with dilate, which means to widen.

items: Indication = reason to use; contraindication = reason not to; adverse = harmful.
Routes: oral mouth, sublingual under tongue, buccal cheek, topical surface, transdermal through skin.
Subcutaneous under skin, intramuscular muscle, intravenous vein; parenteral = not via the gut.
Efficacy = it works; potent = strong; tolerance = weaker response; dependence = needs the drug.
Prescribe orders, proscribe forbids; dilute weakens, dilate widens.

summary: You can now read why a drug is or is not given, where it enters the body, and what it does. You can also separate the HESI A2 sound-alikes: prescribe and proscribe, adverse and averse, efficacy and efficiency, dilute and dilate.

A.q: The nurse explained that the antibiotic would be given by the oral route. What is the best definition of the word "oral" in this sentence?

whyNot.0: The ear is aural, the oral sound-alike.
whyNot.3: An injection is a parenteral route, not oral.

A.q: Which word means "into or within a muscle"?
A.why: Intramuscular means into or within a muscle (intra- = within).

A.q: Before stitching the cut, the doctor injected a local anesthetic around the wound. What is the best definition of the word "anesthetic" in this sentence?
A.why: An anesthetic causes loss of sensation; a local anesthetic numbs one area.

whyNot.1: Killing germs on skin is the job of an antiseptic.
whyNot.2: Lowering fever is the job of an antipyretic.
whyNot.3: Stopping bleeding fits a cut loosely, but it is not what an anesthetic does.

B.q: Mr. Allen's dependence on opioid pain pills began after his back surgery. What is the best definition of the word "dependence" in this sentence?
options: a weaker response to the pills
an allergic reaction to the pills
a need for the pills to function
a refusal to take the pills
B.why: Dependence is a state of needing a drug to function normally.

whyNot.0: A weaker response is tolerance, the classic dependence look-alike.
whyNot.1: An allergy is an immune reaction.
whyNot.3: Refusing the pills is the opposite of depending on them.

B.q: The nurse practitioner will prescribe an inhaler for Ana's asthma. What is the best definition of the word "prescribe" in this sentence?
options: to give the first dose of
B.why: Prescribe means to order the use of a medicine or treatment.

whyNot.1: Forbidding is proscribe, the prescribe sound-alike.
whyNot.2: Explaining fits the sentence loosely, but prescribe means to order.

B.q: The pharmacist told Mr. Cho to dilute the liquid medicine in a glass of water. What is the best definition of the word "dilute" in this sentence?
B.why: Dilute means to make weaker by adding liquid.

whyNot.0: Measuring fits the instruction loosely, but dilute means to weaken with liquid.
whyNot.2: Widening is dilate, the dilute sound-alike.
whyNot.3: Cooling is not the meaning of dilute.

C.q: The concentrated form of the drug must be drawn up with a special syringe. What is the best definition of the word "concentrated" in this sentence?
C.why: Concentrated means containing a large amount of a substance in a given volume: strong.

whyNot.0: Source is not the meaning of concentrated.
whyNot.1: Diluted is the opposite of concentrated.
whyNot.3: Storage temperature fits a drug label loosely, but it is not the meaning.

C.q: Because the patient kept vomiting, the antibiotic was switched to the intravenous route. What is the best definition of the word "intravenous" in this sentence?
C.why: Intravenous means into or within a vein (intra- = within, ven = vein).

C.q: An antiseptic was applied to the skin before the blood draw. What is the best definition of the word "antiseptic" in this sentence?
options: an agent that numbs the skin
an agent that kills germs on skin
an agent that dries the skin
C.why: An antiseptic is a substance applied to living tissue to prevent infection.

whyNot.0: Numbing is the job of an anesthetic, a look-alike word.
whyNot.3: Some antiseptics dry the skin, but that is a side effect, not the meaning.

reteach.title: Routes as ways into a building
reteach.question: If a drug is a visitor trying to get into a building (the body), which door does each route word name?

blocks.body: Oral is the front door: in by mouth and through the hallway of the gut. Sublingual and buccal are side windows in the mouth that skip the hallway. Topical stays on the outside wall. Transdermal seeps through the wall. Injections (subcutaneous, intramuscular, intravenous) are doors cut straight into the building. Every door that skips the gut hallway is parenteral.

blocks.text: Paint on the wall (topical) acts where it is put. Seeping through the wall (transdermal) carries the drug into the blood. Two different doors.

explain.body: An indication is a reason to give a drug. A contraindication is a reason not to (contra- = against). An adverse reaction is a harmful effect.

test.q: Which word names a reason to use a particular treatment?
test.why: An indication is a reason to use a particular treatment.

whyNot.0: A contraindication is a reason not to use it.
whyNot.1: A complication is a new problem that arises during an illness or its treatment.
whyNot.3: Induction means bringing something about, such as inducing labor; it only looks like indication.

explain.body: Oral = by mouth. Sublingual = under the tongue. Buccal = inside the cheek. Topical = on a surface. Transdermal = through the skin.

test.q: Which route word means the drug is placed inside the cheek?
test.why: Buccal means relating to the cheek or the inside of the cheek.

whyNot.0: Sublingual means under the tongue, the other mouth route.
whyNot.2: Topical means on a body surface such as the skin.

explain.body: Efficacy = the drug produces the intended effect. Potent = strong. Tolerance = a weaker response over time. Dependence = needing the drug to function.

test.q: Which word means "the ability to produce the intended effect"?
test.why: Efficacy is the ability to produce the intended effect.

whyNot.1: Efficiency means doing something with little waste.
whyNot.2: Tolerance is a reduced response to a drug.
whyNot.3: Dosage is the amount and timing of a medicine.

explain.body: Analgesic = relieves pain. Anesthetic = loss of sensation. Antipyretic = reduces fever. Antiseptic = prevents infection on living tissue. Placebo = inactive substance.

test.q: Lena took an analgesic for the headache that followed her flu shot. What is the best definition of the word "analgesic" in this sentence?
test.why: An analgesic is a drug that relieves pain.

whyNot.0: A fever reducer is an antipyretic.
whyNot.1: An allergy medicine is an antihistamine; it does not relieve a headache.
whyNot.2: A germ killer is an antiseptic or antibiotic.
